images.prompt: Photorealistic macro photograph of a handcrafted miniature tabletop diorama. A compact matte graphite projector about the size of a toaster sits on the left of a pale neutral tabletop, its lens barrel machined with fine rings and its vents crisp. It casts a soft beam to the right onto a small freestanding screen of stretched ivory paper on a slim graphite stand. The projected image is a simple arrangement of soft pale rectangles, but its right edge runs a finger width past the screen and lands on the backdrop behind. Around the screen sits a thin acid-lime frame outline, marking the area the image is meant to fill. A folded ivory card lies beside the projector, and faint dust floats in the beam. Everything else is calm and aligned. Wide 16:9 landscape frame. The hero object sits slightly left of centre on the lower third, with the related objects extending to the right so the workflow reads left to right. Clean, generous negative space above. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Materials are limited and tactile: heavyweight ivory cotton paper and card with visible fibres, soft folds and slightly deckled edges; matte, bead-blasted graphite metal with fine machining lines, chamfered edges and tiny hex fasteners; frosted acrylic with milky edges and a soft internal glow; sandblasted frosted glass. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Colour palette is restrained and nearly monochrome: white #FFFFFF, warm ivory, pale neutral #F3F5F2, soft grey-green #DCE1DA, muted graphite #626A64 and deep graphite #191D1B. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: one large soft key light from the upper left at about 45 degrees, like diffused north-window daylight, with a gentle white bounce fill from the right; soft grounded contact shadows fall to the lower right. Camera: 100mm macro lens at f/4, eye level with the tabletop, three-quarter view. The hero object is tack sharp and the background melts into smooth, creamy blur on a seamless pale neutral sweep. Mood: calm, precise, orderly and quietly premium, like high-end editorial product photography. Strictly no people, figures, faces, hands or silhouettes. No readable text, letters, numbers, clock digits, logos, signage or user-interface graphics anywhere. No holograms, floating screens, robots with faces, dense cable tangles, carnival or circus elements, cartoon or plastic CGI look, oversaturated colour, lens flare or heavy vignette.

Photorealistic macro photograph of a handcrafted miniature tabletop diorama, captured mid-disaster. The same graphite projector has tilted back on one foot, its lens now pointing high. The beam has swollen far beyond the ivory paper screen: pale rectangles slide across the backdrop, bend over its top edge and stretch across the tabletop in warped trapezoids. The acid-lime frame around the screen still marks the correct size, now holding only a small corner of the image. The paper screen itself has bowed forward and torn from one top clip, its free corner frozen mid-flap, and its graphite stand is sliding sideways. Folded cards stacked nearby have been knocked over by the tipping projector and fan across the table. Dust churns in the brightened beam, every distortion traceable back to the lens. Wide 16:9 landscape frame, same layout and angle as the calm version of this scene. The hero object stays slightly left of centre, and the spread of the disaster runs to the right and toward the camera so its path can be traced back to the source. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Materials are limited and tactile: heavyweight ivory cotton paper and card with visible fibres, soft folds and slightly deckled edges; matte, bead-blasted graphite metal with fine machining lines, chamfered edges and tiny hex fasteners; frosted acrylic with milky edges and a soft internal glow; sandblasted frosted glass. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Colour palette is restrained and nearly monochrome: white #FFFFFF, warm ivory, pale neutral #F3F5F2, soft grey-green #DCE1DA, muted graphite #626A64 and deep graphite #191D1B. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: the same soft upper-left key and right-side bounce fill as a calm studio setup, unchanged, so the disorder reads as physical and real rather than theatrical. Airborne paper, grains and fragments catch the key light with crisp edge highlights. Camera: 85mm lens at f/5.6, same three-quarter tabletop angle, fast shutter freezing everything mid-air. Focus sits where the chain reaction started, and the spread softens into the depth of field. Mood: absurd but plausible, an orderly system that got out of hand, still clean and editorial. Photorealistic photograph of a vast handcrafted miniature landscape diorama. A vast salt flat, bright and cracked into pale polygons, stretches to a sharp horizon under a flat sky. On the left, the building-sized graphite projector lies on its side, lens barrel half buried in crusted salt, vents choked with drifted grit. Across the flat stretches the torn ivory paper screen like a collapsed canopy, draped between two leaning graphite poles, its surface weathered, frayed and scored by wind, with scraps pinned in the salt crust far into the distance. In the midground, a slim graphite rail cart carrying a tall acid-lime tensioning frame is re-stretching one clean panel of the screen, its clamps pulling the paper taut and square, while a small frosted acrylic lens on a graphite tripod aims a narrow beam that fits the panel exactly. Wide 16:9 panoramic frame. The main ruin anchors the left or centre foreground, terrain rolls back to a distant horizon on the upper third, and the lime recovery rig sits in the right midground. Shot as a real physical model, not a 3D render. Surfaces carry believable imperfections: fine dust, paper grain, hairline creases, light scuffs on metal. Every object has convincing miniature scale and weight and rests firmly on its surface. Acid lime #D0F344 appears only on the lime element named in the scene, as the single signal colour, with olive #718D0B on its shadowed sides. Nothing else is lime or saturated; no red, orange or blue accents. Lighting: soft overcast late-afternoon daylight still falling from the upper left, with long soft shadows grounding the ruins and atmospheric haze fading distant forms into pale grey-green.
